unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Year 7 English at Ehel Academy! This is Unit 1: Family, Identity, and History. In this unit, you will explore some of the most important questions a person can ask: Where do I come from? Who are the people in my family? What stories have been passed down through the generations? You will read about families, learn how to describe your own background, and discover how people across East Africa and the wider world have moved, settled, and built new lives over the centuries.
unit.learningPath: Begin with the five vocabulary groups and learn the thirty unit words a few at a time, saying each example sentence aloud. Read the introduction to oral history, then "The Journey of Alina's Family" and the two-part story "The Fire Behind the Fence", answering the comprehension questions with evidence from the text. Work through the six grammar lessons, from the past simple tense to editing and application. Complete the writing workshop, beginning with your family biography, then record the speaking tasks, finish the activities and the quiz, and close with the Check Your Learning self-assessment.
howToUse: Start with the five vocabulary groups — thirty words in all — a few at a time, and say every example sentence aloud.

Read in this order: the introduction to oral history, “Keeping the Story Alive”; then “The Journey of Alina's Family”; then “The Fire Behind the Fence”, parts 1 and 2. Answer the comprehension questions with evidence from the text.
The writing workshop begins with your own family biography, and Speaking 1 is presenting it — do the writing first.

readings.title: Keeping the Story Alive: Oral History and Heritage
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Family is at the heart of every culture. In Somali culture, for example, knowing your ancestry is deeply important, and many people can name their great-great-grandparents and trace their family line back through many generations. This tradition of reciting the family line is called abtirsiinyo, and some people can recite twenty generations or more. It helps a person know their ancestry, their clan, and their place in the community. In other East African communities, family histories are kept alive through oral stories, songs, and special objects passed from one generation to the next.
Historians use several precise words for the ways families remember. Oral history means stories and knowledge passed down by speaking rather than by writing, often from a grandparent to a grandchild. An artifact is an object made by people in the past, such as a carved stool, a woven basket, or a faded photograph, and families often treasure such objects for the memories they hold. A chronicle is a record of events written in the order they happened, and a legacy is what a person leaves behind: values, achievements, skills, or property. Each generation adds its own chapter to the record, and a descendant who listens carefully inherits far more than a name.
Why does any of this matter? When people experience migration, moving from one place to another in search of safety or a better life, they often lose houses, land, and possessions along the way. What survives the journey is usually the story itself. A family that knows its heritage carries its identity anywhere, because heritage lives in memory and language as much as in objects.
Read this interview with Amara, a student whose family history shows exactly how such stories survive.
Interviewer: Amara, can you tell us about your family's history?
Amara: Of course. My family originally came from a farming region in southern Ethiopia. My great-grandfather owned a piece of land where he grew coffee and maize. He married young and had twelve children.
Interviewer: That is a big family! What happened next?
Amara: In the 1960s, there was a drought. The crops failed, and the family struggled to survive. My grandfather decided to leave the farm. He took his wife and four children and walked for three weeks to reach the city. It was an incredibly difficult migration.
Interviewer: How did the family manage in the city?
Amara: It was hard at first. My grandfather worked as a porter at the market. My grandmother sold spices from a small table. Slowly, they saved money and opened a shop. My father grew up in that shop, and he always said it was the heart of the family.
Interviewer: What is the most important thing you learned from your family's story?
Amara: That heritage is not about wealth or possessions. It is about the strength and courage your family showed when life was hard. My grandfather's legacy is not the shop — it is the lesson that hard work and family always come first.
As you work through this unit, you will read a longer family story, study the past simple tense that storytellers depend on, and finally write a biography of someone in your own family. Notice how Amara uses past simple verbs such as came, owned, grew, married, walked, and opened to describe completed events. By the end of the unit, you will be able to do the same for the people whose journeys made your life possible.

readings.title: The Journey of Alina's Family
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Alina sat on the floor of her grandmother's sitting room in Hargeisa, her legs crossed beneath her. The evening air carried the smell of bariis iyo hilib from the kitchen. Ayeeyo settled into her favourite chair and smiled.
"You want to know about our family?" Ayeeyo asked. "Then listen carefully, because this story travelled across deserts and seas before it reached you."
Ayeeyo began with her own grandfather, a man named Zane. Zane lived in a small village near the coast in the early 1900s. He belonged to a well-known clan that traded goods along the Indian Ocean. Zane worked as a boat-builder. He crafted vessels from local timber and sold them to merchants who sailed between Berbera and Aden.
"When Zane grew older," Ayeeyo explained, "he married a woman named Alina from a farming family inland. They moved to a town near the mountains and raised seven children. One of those children was my father, your great-grandfather, Nadir."
Nadir studied at a small school where he learned reading, arithmetic and the languages of trade. Later, he travelled to Aden for work. He spent five years there and saved enough money to return home and open a small shop. He married a woman called Sana, and together they had eight children.
"Your grandmother — that is me — was the youngest," Ayeeyo said, laughing. "I grew up hearing stories about Zane and the boats he built. My father kept a piece of old rope from one of those boats in a wooden box. It was our family's most precious artifact."
When conflict erupted in the region in the late 1980s, Ayeeyo's family faced a difficult choice. They packed what they could carry and joined thousands of others in a long migration south. They walked for days. They slept under trees. They arrived in a refugee camp exhausted but alive.
"We lost many things," Ayeeyo said quietly. "But we never lost our story. Every night in the camp, I told your mother the same stories my father told me. That is our heritage — it lives in words, not in objects."
Years later, the family resettled and rebuilt their lives. Alina's mother studied hard, became a nurse, and moved to Hargeisa. She named her daughter Alina after Zane's wife — the first Alina — to honour the ancestry that connected them all.
Alina looked at her grandmother. "So I am a descendant of a boat-builder?"
Ayeeyo nodded. "And a trader, a farmer, a scholar, and a survivor. You carry all of them inside you. That is what family means — a legacy that never disappears, even when everything else changes."
That night, Alina opened her notebook and wrote the first line of her family chronicle: "My name is Alina, and this is the story of where I come from."

readings.title: The Fire Behind the Fence, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Jamal stood at the edge of the dusty football field, his fists clenched. The sun was setting, casting long shadows across the small apartment buildings in their Nairobi neighbourhood. The field was the only open space nearby, a place where joy and rivalry mixed like dust and sweat. Today, however, it had become a battlefield.
"They argue too much," whispered Ben beside him. "And now they want to fight."
Across the field, another group of boys had gathered. Their leader, Kofi, was known for being belligerent. He walked with a swagger and often shouted orders. Jamal remembered when Kofi used to be friendly. But something had changed over the past few months.
It all started with an argument about football. Jamal's team claimed Kofi's group had broken the goalpost, which Kofi denied. The conflict grew quickly. Words turned into shouting. Then came threats. The air between them became thick with animosity.
Kofi stepped forward, his chin up. "This is our field. You lost it when you lied about the post."
"You're the liar," Jamal said sharply. "Your whole team is just devious and loud."
Kofi's jaw clenched. "Say that again."
"You heard me," Jamal replied.
Max, Kofi's friend, stepped forward. "We should retaliate," he muttered. "Let them know who really owns this field."
Jamal's stomach tightened. He didn't want to fight. But walking away felt like losing. His father once said, "You shouldn't let others walk over you." But his mother always told him, "You should stay calm and choose peace."
That night, Jamal lay awake, the sounds of Nairobi's night outside his window. He thought about what his grandfather had told him: "Revenge is like a fire in dry grass — it spreads fast, but leaves only ash."
The next morning, everything changed.
A neighbour's house caught fire. Smoke billowed above the buildings. Jamal and others ran toward the fire. When he reached the house, he was shocked to see Kofi inside the smoky yard, trying to free a goat tied to a wooden fence.
"Kofi!" Jamal screamed. "Get out of there!"
Kofi didn't listen. He kicked at the fence until it broke. The goat bolted. Jamal ran to help Kofi, grabbing his arm just as part of the fence fell behind them.
Afterward, they sat on the curb, coughing and covered in ash.
"You could've died," Jamal said.
Kofi shrugged. "The goat didn't do anything wrong. I had to try."
People around the neighbourhood praised Kofi's bravery. Jamal began to see him differently. Maybe the boy who shouted and pushed people wasn't all bad. Maybe there was more behind his abrasive mask.
But peace was short-lived.
A week later, Jamal returned from school to find his football slashed open. A knife mark ran right through it. His anger flared like dry kindling. He knew exactly who had done it.
He stormed across the field, the ruined ball in hand. "You think you're funny?" he shouted at Kofi.
"What are you talking about?" Kofi looked genuinely confused.
"Don't act innocent," Jamal said. "Only someone as vindictive as you would do this."
Kofi frowned. "It wasn't me. You're always so quick to blame. You're becoming as abrasive as your team."
"You're just trying to antagonize me again!"
Kofi's face hardened. "You're full of malevolence. You want me punished."
Their shouting drew a crowd. A teacher walking by came over.

readings.title: The Fire Behind the Fence, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
"Enough," she said. "What's going on?"
Jamal showed her the torn ball. "He destroyed it."
"I didn't," Kofi replied. "He's always defiant, never listens."
The teacher made them sit on the nearby bench. "You should speak honestly, not throw blame. Talk."
They sat in silence. Then Kofi said, "I really didn't do it. Maybe someone else wants us to fight."
Jamal's anger began to cool. "But who?"
That evening, Ben came running with something in his hand — a knife with the initials M.O. carved into the handle.
"Milo Otieno!" Jamal gasped. Milo had once been on their team but felt left out. He had stopped coming to play, and lately, he had been making derogatory remarks from the edge of the field, trying to jeer at the players.
"He used to say we treated him unfairly," Kofi remembered. "Maybe he did this to exacerbate our conflict."
They went to Milo's house. When they confronted him, he tried to connive his way out.
"That's not mine," he said, his eyes shifting.
"Don't be mendacious," Jamal replied. "It has your initials."
Milo sighed. "Fine. I did it. I just... I felt left out. You all stopped talking to me. I was angry."
"You could've talked to us," Jamal said. "You shouldn't have done this."
"Can I still play?" Milo asked.
Kofi hesitated. "Only if you're honest. No more tricks. No more lies."
Milo nodded quickly. "I promise."
In the weeks that followed, things slowly changed. Milo rejoined the group. Kofi and Jamal became better at talking before shouting. Whenever small problems came up, they tried to solve them with words.
One afternoon, Jamal and Kofi sat on the field's edge, watching the younger boys practise.
"Remember how angry we used to get?" Jamal asked.
"We were hotheads," Kofi said, laughing. "But I guess we were just kids with too much pride."
Jamal smiled. "Yeah. Pride and no patience."
Kofi nodded. "But we've learned. And we're better for it."
Behind them, Ben called out, "Hey, captains! We need you for the next game."
Jamal and Kofi stood up. They looked at each other and grinned. Not long ago, they were enemies. Now, they were leaders.
And they weren't just leading a game anymore. They were leading by example.
Even in moments of tension, they reminded others, "You should stay calm." When younger players began to argue, they guided them to talk. When someone felt alienated, they made space. They organised a weekend clean-up of the field, inviting everyone — including those who used to be rivals.
The field changed, and so did the boys. Kofi, once narcissistic and loud, now listened before speaking. Jamal, once quick to anger, now paused and considered. The old discrepancy between them faded, replaced by respect.
One day, a new student tried to harass Milo during practice. Jamal stepped in immediately. "That's not how we treat each other here," he said firmly. "You shouldn't bring problems from outside to our team."
The student backed down, surprised.
Later that evening, Jamal told Kofi, "I used to think the biggest problem was losing a ball or a match. But now I see — it's losing trust."
Kofi nodded slowly. "And once trust breaks, it takes a lot to fix it. But we did."
And the field, once a place of battles, became a place of healing.

grammar.title: The Past Simple Tense
grammar.explanation: The past simple tense describes actions and events that started and finished in the past, which makes it the storyteller's tense. Almost every sentence in a biography, a family history or a chronicle depends on it, so this unit treats it as your most important tool.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Regular verbs add -ed to the base form: work → worked, pack → packed, settle → settled, travel → travelled (double the final consonant), study → studied (change y to i), live → lived (just add -d). Irregular verbs must be memorised: go → went, sit → sat, grow → grew, build → built, have → had, tell → told, write → wrote, begin → began, lose → lost, sleep → slept, become → became, spend → spent.
The reading passage shows the tense at work: "Zane lived in a small village near the coast." "He worked as a boat-builder." "They packed what they could carry." "She named her daughter Alina after Zane's wife."
Negatives use did not (didn't) + base form: "She did not lose her story", never "did not lost". Questions put did before the subject with the base form: "Did Zane build boats?", never "Did Zane built?"
Time markers that signal the past simple include yesterday, last week, in 1990, in the early 1900s, three days ago, once and at that time.
grammar.commonMistake: Mixing the present into a past story ("He live in a village" should be "He lived in a village"), inventing regular forms for irregular verbs ("She goed" should be "She went"), and keeping the past form after did ("Did he worked?" should be "Did he work?"). Only did carries the past in negatives and questions.
grammar.memoryTip: Base form + -ed covers every regular verb; for the irregular ones, make flashcards with the base form on one side and the past form on the other. The fifty most common irregular verbs cover about ninety per cent of everyday speech, so a few minutes of practice each day pays off quickly.
grammar.practice:
Part A — write the past simple form of each verb and mark it (R) regular or (I) irregular: 1) walk 2) go 3) study 4) build 5) live 6) tell 7) travel 8) begin 9) marry 10) sleep 11) eat 12) see. Part B — complete each sentence with the past simple of the verb in brackets: 1) Alina ______ (sit) on the floor and ______ (listen) to her grandmother. 2) Zane ______ (craft) boats from local timber. 3) The family ______ (move) to a town near the mountains. 4) Nadir ______ (spend) five years in Aden. 5) They ______ (pack) what they could carry and ______ (leave). 6) Ayeeyo ______ (tell) stories every night in the camp. 7) Alina's mother ______ (study) hard and ______ (become) a nurse. 8) They ______ (visit) their grandparents last summer. 9) He ______ (see) a colourful bird in the garden. Part C — rewrite each sentence as a negative using did not: 1) She walked to school yesterday. 2) They arrived on time. 3) He told his friend the secret. 4) The family lost their story. Part D — rewrite each sentence as a question using did: 1) Zane built boats near the coast. 2) The family moved to a new town. 3) Nadir studied at a small school. 4) Alina wrote in her notebook.

===
Answer Key (self-check) — Part A: 1) walked (R) 2) went (I) 3) studied (R) 4) built (I) 5) lived (R) 6) told (I) 7) travelled (R) 8) began (I) 9) married (R) 10) slept (I) 11) ate (I) 12) saw (I). Part B: 1) sat, listened 2) crafted 3) moved 4) spent 5) packed, left 6) told 7) studied, became 8) visited 9) saw. Part C: 1) She did not walk to school yesterday. 2) They did not arrive on time. 3) He did not tell his friend the secret. 4) The family did not lose their story. Part D: 1) Did Zane build boats near the coast? 2) Did the family move to a new town? 3) Did Nadir study at a small school? 4) Did Alina write in her notebook?

grammar.title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
grammar.explanation: Both tenses look back, but they answer different questions. The past simple pins an event to a finished time, while the present perfect connects a past action to the present moment. Choosing between them is one of the most important decisions a Grade 7 writer makes.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Use the past simple for finished actions at a stated time, usually with markers such as yesterday, last week, in 2010 or three years ago: "I visited my cousins last summer." "She lived in Nairobi for five years" (she no longer lives there). Form the present perfect with have or has + past participle for experiences with no stated time, or for situations that continue now: "I have visited the coast" (at some point in my life). "She has lived in Nairobi for five years" (she still lives there). Compare the pair: "I saw that film last night" names the time, so it takes the past simple; "I have seen that film before" names no time, so it takes the present perfect.
grammar.commonMistake: Attaching the present perfect to a finished time ("I have visited Aden last summer" should be "I visited Aden last summer") and dropping the auxiliary ("She gone to the shop" should be "She has gone to the shop").
grammar.memoryTip: Past simple answers "What did you do?"; present perfect answers "What have you done?" If the question "When?" has an exact answer, choose the past simple; if the honest answer is "at some point", choose the present perfect.
grammar.practice:
Choose the correct tense and write the full sentence: 1) I ______ (visit) my grandmother last weekend. 2) She ______ (never / see) a lion before. 3) They ______ (play) football yesterday. 4) We ______ (be) to the beach many times. 5) He ______ (live) in Hargeisa since 2015. 6) My family ______ (move) to this city in 2010. Then write two sentences of your own about your family: one past simple sentence with a time marker, and one present perfect sentence about an experience that still matters today.

===
Answer Key (self-check) — 1) I visited my grandmother last weekend. (past simple: stated time, "last weekend") 2) She has never seen a lion before. (present perfect: no stated time, "before") 3) They played football yesterday. (past simple: stated time, "yesterday") 4) We have been to the beach many times. (present perfect: experience, no stated time) 5) He has lived in Hargeisa since 2015. (present perfect: "since" links the past to now) 6) My family moved to this city in 2010. (past simple: stated time, "in 2010"). The closing task (two original sentences about your own family) is open-ended — there is no single correct answer. Self-check by modelling your sentences on the explanation's own pattern: a past-simple sentence with a clear time marker (e.g. "My grandfather moved to Berbera in 1998.") and a present-perfect sentence about an experience with no stated time that still matters today (e.g. "My family has kept this tradition for three generations."). Confirm the past-simple sentence names a finished time and the present-perfect sentence names none.

grammar.title: Apostrophes for Possession
grammar.explanation: An apostrophe turns a noun into an owner, which lets one word do the work of a whole phrase: "the traditions of the families" becomes "the families' traditions". Because a misplaced apostrophe changes who owns what, accuracy here keeps your family biography clear.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Singular owners add 's: the boy's kite, Alina's notebook, my grandmother's house. Plural owners that already end in s add only the apostrophe: the boys' kites, the families' traditions, the teachers' meeting. Irregular plurals that do not end in s behave like singulars and add 's: the children's books, the men's team, the women's plan. The apostrophe's position tells the reader how many owners there are: my brother's plans belong to one brother, while my brothers' plans belong to more than one.
grammar.commonMistake: Leaving the apostrophe out ("the cats toy" should be "the cat's toy") and, just as often, forcing one into an ordinary plural ("The boy's are playing" should be "The boys are playing" — no ownership means no apostrophe).
grammar.memoryTip: Ask two questions: does something belong to someone, and how many owners are there? Ownership earns the apostrophe, and the owner count decides whether it lands before or after the s.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each phrase with the apostrophe in the correct place: 1) the ______ (dog) collar — one dog. 2) the ______ (girls) dresses — many girls. 3) the ______ (teacher) pen — one teacher. 4) the ______ (children) playground — many children. 5) my ______ (grandmother) stories — one grandmother. 6) the ______ (families) houses — many families. Then write two sentences about your own family that each use a possessive apostrophe: one with a single owner and one with plural owners.

===
Answer Key (self-check) — 1) the dog's collar 2) the girls' dresses 3) the teacher's pen 4) the children's playground (irregular plural, takes 's like a singular) 5) my grandmother's stories 6) the families' houses. The closing task (two original sentences about your own family, one with a single owner and one with plural owners) is open-ended — there is no single correct answer. Self-check using the rule: a singular owner takes 's (e.g. "My father's job is in Garowe.") and a plural owner already ending in -s takes only the apostrophe (e.g. "My cousins' house is near the river."). Confirm each apostrophe's position matches how many owners you named.

grammar.title: Defining Relative Clauses
grammar.explanation: A defining relative clause adds essential identifying information straight after a noun, so the reader knows exactly which person, thing or place you mean. In a family biography it lets you pack history into one sentence: "The man who lives in Mogadishu is my uncle."
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Choose the pronoun by what you are describing: who for people ("The man who lives next door is a teacher"), which for things ("The book which I borrowed was fascinating"), that for people or things in informal writing ("The boy that scored the goal is my friend"), whose for possession ("The girl whose father is a doctor wants to study medicine") and where for places ("The village where my grandmother grew up is very small"). Place the clause directly after the noun it defines, and never wrap a defining clause in commas. To build one, combine two short sentences: "The man is my uncle" and "He lives in Mogadishu" become "The man who lives in Mogadishu is my uncle."
grammar.commonMistake: Using who for things ("The car who is red" should be "The car that is red") and adding commas around information the sentence cannot spare ("The boy, who runs fast, is my brother" should be "The boy who runs fast is my brother" when the clause identifies which boy).
grammar.memoryTip: Who = people, which and that = things, whose = possession, where = places. If removing the clause leaves the reader asking "which one?", the clause is defining — keep the commas away.
grammar.practice:
Complete each sentence with who, which, that, whose or where: 1) The woman ______ lives next door is very kind. 2) This is the book ______ I borrowed from the library. 3) I know a boy ______ father works at the hospital. 4) The village ______ my family came from is near the coast. 5) The cat ______ sleeps on the sofa is mine. Then join each pair into one sentence with a defining relative clause: 6) My aunt is a nurse. + She works in Hargeisa. 7) The box held old rope. + The rope came from a fishing boat.

===
Answer Key (self-check) — 1) who (person) 2) which, or that in informal writing (thing) 3) whose (possession) 4) where (place) 5) that, or which (the cat is not a person, so who does not apply) 6) My aunt who works in Hargeisa is a nurse. 7) The box held old rope which (or that) came from a fishing boat. Check each choice against ruleAndExamples: who for people, which/that for things, whose for possession, where for places — and confirm no commas surround the clause, since it identifies which one is meant.

grammar.title: Should / Shouldn't
grammar.explanation: Should and shouldn't give advice and make recommendations: should marks a wise choice, and shouldn't warns against a poor one. In "The Fire Behind the Fence", almost every turning point arrives as advice built on these two words.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Positive advice: subject + should + base verb — "You should listen to your friend." "He should apologise." Negative advice: subject + shouldn't + base verb — "You shouldn't shout during a disagreement." "She shouldn't ignore the problem." Questions: should + subject + base verb — "Should I talk to my teacher about it?" "Should we try to solve this together?" The story models all of these: "You shouldn't let others walk over you." "You should stay calm and choose peace." "You should speak honestly, not throw blame." "You shouldn't have done this."
grammar.commonMistake: Putting a past form after should ("You should told the truth" should be "You should tell the truth") — should itself never changes, and the verb after it stays in the base form.
grammar.memoryTip: Should = this is a good idea; shouldn't = this is a bad idea. Whatever follows either word is always the bare base form of the verb.
grammar.practice:
Complete each sentence with should or shouldn't: 1) If you are feeling upset, you ______ talk to someone you trust. 2) You ______ be rude to your classmates. 3) When you make a mistake, you ______ admit it. 4) You ______ keep your promises to your friends. 5) If someone antagonizes you, you ______ try to stay calm. 6) You ______ spread rumours about other people. Then write two sentences of advice for Milo from the story: one with should and one with shouldn't.

===
Answer Key (self-check) — 1) should 2) shouldn't 3) should 4) should 5) should 6) shouldn't. The closing task (two original sentences of advice for Milo) is open-ended — there is no single fixed answer. Ground your self-check in the story itself: Milo damaged the ball because he felt left out and angry after the other boys stopped talking to him, and once he confessed he asked whether he could still play with the team. A well-formed answer follows the pattern already modelled in ruleAndExamples ("You should stay calm and choose peace." / "You shouldn't let others walk over you."), for example "You should tell your friends when you feel left out." and "You shouldn't damage things when you are angry." Confirm each sentence uses should or shouldn't followed by the bare base form of the verb.

grammar.title: Grade 7 Editing and Application
grammar.explanation: Strong writers finish by editing: they reread a complete draft and check that every past simple verb, apostrophe and relative clause actually does its job. Editing is where this unit's grammar stops being a set of rules and becomes your own voice.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Work through one feature at a time rather than hunting everything at once. First pass: are all completed past events in the past simple, with irregular verbs in their correct forms? Second pass: does every possessive apostrophe sit before or after the s to match the number of owners? Third pass: does at least one defining relative clause add essential detail without commas? Final pass: read the draft aloud and listen for sentences that run on or stop short.
grammar.commonMistake: Changing words during revision without rereading the whole sentence, so the paragraph slowly drifts away from its meaning. After every edit, reread the full sentence and ask whether it still says what you intended.
grammar.memoryTip: Edit in passes: verbs first, apostrophes second, clauses third, sound last. Read, notice, revise, reread.
grammar.practice:
Write six sentences about your family's past, then edit them with the unit checklist: 1) where a family member grew up, using an irregular verb; 2) work a relative did, using a regular verb; 3) a journey or move your family made, with a time marker such as "in 2010"; 4) a tradition your family kept, using the word heritage; 5) a negative sentence about something that did not happen; 6) a question you would like to ask an older relative. Finally, check every sentence for capital letters, end punctuation, correct past simple forms and at least one possessive apostrophe across the set.

===
Answer Key (self-check): this task is open-ended personal composition — there is no single correct answer, since it asks you to write about your own family. Use this model set to self-check the shape each sentence should take (swap in your own family's real details): 1) "My grandmother grew up in a small fishing village." (irregular verb: grow → grew) 2) "My uncle worked as a teacher for twenty years." (regular verb: work → worked) 3) "My family moved to this city in 2010." (a journey or move, with a time marker) 4) "We keep our heritage alive by cooking my great-grandmother's recipes every year." (uses the word heritage) 5) "My father did not grow up in this town." (negative with did not) 6) "What was your childhood like, Grandma?" (a question for an older relative). Then run the four edit passes from ruleAndExamples over your own six sentences: verbs (past simple, irregular forms correct), apostrophes (position matches the number of owners), at least one defining relative clause with no surrounding commas, and a final read-aloud check for capital letters and end punctuation.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Where Do You Come From? Game

Swap roles and replay the scene between Milo and the team.

writing.title: Writing 1: My Family Biography
writing.promptAndInstructions: Plan and write a family biography — a true story about a member of your family or your family's history. Choose your subject: a grandparent and their early life, a parent's journey to where you live now, a relative who did something remarkable, or your family's migration story. Gather information first by asking questions such as "Where were you born?", "What was life like when you were a child?" and "What challenges did the family face?" Then write five paragraphs: an introduction naming the person and one striking fact; their early life; the most important events of their life, with time markers such as "in 1980"; the legacy and lessons they passed on; and a personal conclusion about what their story means to you. Include at least eight past simple verbs (three of them irregular), five vocabulary words from this unit, one defining relative clause, two possessive apostrophes and one time marker. Aim for 250 to 350 words, and read your work aloud before you finish.
writing.modelText: My grandfather, Aran, was born in 1948 in a small town called Burao. He grew up in a large family with six brothers and three sisters. His father worked as a livestock trader who travelled between towns along the northern plains. Aran's mother, whose name was Dina, kept the household together while her husband was away, and my grandfather always said that his mother's strength was the foundation of the whole family.
writing.sentenceStarter: The person I have chosen to write about is...
writing.successCriteria: I introduced my subject clearly; organised the biography into five cohesive paragraphs; used at least eight past simple verbs and five unit words; included a defining relative clause and two possessive apostrophes; checked punctuation; revised my work
writing.support: Interview a relative first, plan one idea per paragraph, then draft with the unit word bank beside you.
writing.extension: Weave in a direct quotation from the person, acknowledge how two relatives remember one event differently, and end with a reflective final line.

writing.title: Writing 2: Retell a Scene from the Story
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose your favourite scene from "The Fire Behind the Fence" — the confrontation, the fire, or the visit to Milo's house — and retell it in your own words in one paragraph of at least five sentences. Use at least three vocabulary words from this unit and keep every verb in the past simple. End with one sentence explaining why this scene matters to the whole story.
writing.modelText: When the neighbour's house caught fire, Kofi ran into the smoky yard because a frightened goat was tied to the fence, and that choice changed everything Jamal believed about him.
writing.expectedLength: One organised paragraph of at least five sentences
writing.successCriteria: I retold the events in my own words and in order; kept every verb in the past simple; included three unit words; explained why the scene matters; checked spelling and punctuation
writing.support: Reread your chosen scene twice, list its events in order, then close the book and retell it from your list.
writing.extension: Retell the same scene from Kofi's point of view and compare how the feeling of the moment changes.

writing.title: Writing 3: A Letter of Advice to Jamal
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine Jamal writes to you just after his football is slashed, before he learns the truth. Write a letter back giving him advice in two paragraphs. Use should at least three times and shouldn't at least three times, and support each piece of advice with a reason. Remind him what his grandfather said about revenge, and suggest one calm step he could take before blaming anyone.
writing.modelText: Dear Jamal, I understand why you feel angry, but you should ask questions before you blame anyone, and you shouldn't let one torn ball destroy a friendship that can still be repaired.
writing.sentenceStarter: Dear Jamal, I was sorry to read about...
writing.expectedLength: Two organised paragraphs in letter form
writing.successCriteria: I wrote in a warm letter format; gave advice with should three times and shouldn't three times; supported each piece of advice with a reason; referred to the story's events accurately; revised my work
writing.support: List your six pieces of advice first, then decide which belong in each paragraph.
writing.extension: Add a third paragraph predicting what might happen if Jamal ignores your advice.

writing.title: Writing 4: Character Comparison — Jamal and Kofi
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write two paragraphs comparing Jamal and Kofi at the beginning of the story and at the end. In the first paragraph, describe how each boy behaved during the quarrel, using vocabulary such as belligerent, defiant and abrasive. In the second, explain how each boy changed after the truth emerged, giving at least two pieces of evidence from the text. Use past simple verbs throughout.
writing.modelText: At the start, Kofi walked with a swagger and shouted orders, while Jamal answered every insult with a sharper one of his own.
writing.sentenceStarter: At the beginning of the story, the two boys...
writing.successCriteria: I compared both boys at the beginning and at the end; supported every claim with evidence from the story; used unit vocabulary precisely; kept verbs in the past simple; checked cohesion between the two paragraphs
writing.support: Make a two-column chart — beginning and end — for each boy before you draft.
writing.extension: Add a final sentence judging which boy changed more, and defend your judgement.

writing.title: Writing 5: A Different Ending
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: What if Ben had never found the knife and Milo had never been discovered? Write a new ending of at least six sentences in one paragraph. Show what happens to the friendship between Jamal and Kofi, keep the characters true to themselves, and use at least two vocabulary words such as animosity, exacerbate or alienate. Keep the narration in the past simple.
writing.modelText: Without the truth, every practice ended in fresh accusations, and the animosity between the two teams grew until nobody wanted to play at all.
writing.sentenceStarter: If the truth had stayed hidden...
writing.expectedLength: One organised paragraph of at least six sentences
writing.successCriteria: I invented a believable ending that follows from the story; kept the characters consistent; used two or more unit words; kept the narration in the past simple; ended with a clear final image or thought
writing.support: Decide first whether the conflict grows or fades, then list three events that lead there.
writing.extension: Write a closing line of dialogue for the teacher that sums up what was lost.

writing.title: Writing 6: A Conflict I Remember
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write about a real disagreement you once had with a friend, classmate or family member — one you are comfortable sharing. In one or two paragraphs, describe what happened, how it was resolved, and what you learned from it. Use the past simple throughout, include at least three vocabulary words from this unit, and finish with one sentence of advice using should or shouldn't.
writing.modelText: Last year I argued with my cousin about a borrowed bicycle, and the silence that followed taught me more than the argument itself ever did.
writing.expectedLength: One or two organised personal paragraphs
writing.successCriteria: I described a real conflict honestly and respectfully; explained how it was resolved; used three unit words; kept the past simple; closed with one sentence of advice using should or shouldn't
writing.support: Answer three planning questions first: what started it, what changed it, what ended it.
writing.extension: Rewrite your final sentence as advice for a younger learner facing the same situation.

teacherNotes.note: Model disciplinary language aloud, teach annotation and source checking explicitly, use mixed-response modes, and give specific feedback on evidence, cohesion, viewpoint and vocabulary precision while increasing learner independence.

Encourage learners to use the AI tutor to rehearse the thirty unit words aloud, to practise each grammar focus (past simple, present perfect versus past simple, possessive apostrophes, defining relative clauses and should or shouldn't), to plan and check the family biography, and to reread "The Fire Behind the Fence" before answering the comprehension questions. Remind families that a parent or caregiver should stay nearby and supervise whenever a learner works online, and that the interview with an older relative in Speaking 5 should be arranged with an adult present.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Look for accurate quotations: past simple lines such as "The goat bolted"; advice lines such as "You should stay calm and choose peace" and "You shouldn't bring problems from outside to our team"; perfect forms "we've learned" and "You shouldn't have done this"; possessives such as Kofi's face, Jamal's team, the neighbour's house and the field's edge.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Angry and ready to fight or argue. The belligerent dog barked loudly at anyone who came near.
The wish to do evil or harm to others. The villain in the story showed malevolence by trying to hurt the hero.
Wanting to hurt someone because they hurt you. After being teased, she felt vindictive and wanted to get back at her classmates.
To make someone very angry. It can infuriate me when people talk during a movie.
belligerent — angry and ready to fight or argue; the narrator uses it to explain Kofi's reputation as a leader.
vindictive — wanting to hurt someone because they hurt you; Jamal hurls the word at Kofi over the slashed ball.
animosity — a strong feeling of dislike or hatred; it describes the poisoned air between the two teams.
narcissistic — very interested in yourself and convinced you are better than others; the ending contrasts it with Kofi's new habit of listening.
argue — to exchange opposing opinions, each side trying to convince the other; Ben whispers it as the two groups face each other.
argument — a disagreement in which people express different opinions; the goalpost argument is the seed of the whole conflict.
